articles.title: Nordic Outlook Update - Euro area
articles.heading: Nordic Outlook (Eng)
articles.fulltext:
Our publication of Nordic Outlook in November has a slightly different format compared to other editions during the year. Under the heading Nordic Outlook Update , we are continuously publishing our forecasts and our macro view for individual countries/regions. On Tuesday 10 November, we will publish our overall view on growth, inflation, interest rates, etc., together with the table of all forecasts. 
Stronger-than-expected growth so far in 2026 will be followed by a temporary slowdown in the end of the year and early 2027. Growth will be supported by household consumption and investment. Higher energy prices will keep inflation elevated for longer, prompting the ECB to raise interest rates in December 2026 and March 2027. As inflation moves closer to target, the ECB will cut rates three times in 2028. Elections in several countries – with parties on the fringes gaining ground – can have major implications for the whole of the EU.  
Indicators such as the PMI point to stronger economic activity while consumer confidence remains low (and weaker than actual consumer behaviour suggests). GDP growth has been resilient so far in 2026, prompting us to an upward revise of our forecast for 2026. However, quarterly growth is expected to slow at the end of 2026 and early 2027 due to higher interest rates and elevated energy prices, in particular natural gas.  
GDP is projected to grow just above 1 per cent in 2026 and slightly below 1.5 per cent in 2027–2028. A solid labour market and rising real disposable income supports consumption. Investment in infrastructure, defence, and to some extent AI, will also support growth. 
The political situation remains highly uncertain, especially in France. Public finances are weak, and substantial fiscal consolidation is needed. At the same time, large-scale demonstrations over poor conditions in schools and economic hardship are adding to pressure for higher public spending. French budget deficit is expected to reach almost 5.5 per cent of GDP this year and the government aims for it to reach around 5 per cent in 2027. However, the weak growth outlook makes this forecast appear rather optimistic. In polls for the presidential election in 2027, far-right and far-left candidate are gaining ground. 
To lift growth above potential around 1.2 per cent the EU needs to make further progress on the reforms proposed in the 2024 Draghi report. Deepening the single market, particularly by integrating capital markets and simplifying regulation, could lift growth.
Energy prices remain high, with price increases broadening this autumn and pushing home energy costs higher. There are still no clear signs of indirect or second-round effects on core inflation, but we expect these to start feeding through in 2027. The extent of these effects will depend on the situation in the Middle East. A resolution of the conflict could ease price pressures and will be key to the inflation outlook for 2028 and for the ECB.
The ECB is concerned about elevated energy prices, indirect effects and second-round effects on wages. If energy prices fall, as markets expect, the policy rate may be on the high side, leaving room for cuts. Rising government bond yields have done much of the tightening. President Lagarde will step down in February 2027. We expect the inflation outlook and economic development to remain decisive for monetary policy, although ECB interpretation and communication may change depending on the composition of the Governing Council.

articles.title: The Riksbank and US midterm elections in focus
articles.heading: The Week Ahead
articles.fulltext:
A very interesting week coming up! The midterm elections, an expected Riksbank hike on Wednesday and Swedish and euro area inflation data will keep us busy. In Norway, Norges Bank is expected to keep rates unchanged amid continued inflation uncertainty.
US:
Midterm elections will be the main event and whether Democrats will reach a majority in both the House of Representatives and the Senate. A likely shift in the House will deadlock fiscal policy and increase pressures to negotiate budget issues. With control of the House, Democrats can force votes on legislation, but they cannot overcome the President’s veto. The President largely retains control of immigration, trade and foreign policy. We will also get key data including ISM manufacturing and services and non-farm payrolls. The US Treasury will announce its quarterly refunding plans.
Euro area: 
Euro area HICP inflation is the key event. Industrial production data for major economies and retail sales for Germany will also be of interest. The ECB wage tracker will be closely watched for signs of second-round effects from higher energy prices. Finally, German industrial orders could shed some light on production in the near term.
Sweden:
A very interesting week with the Riksbank’s rate decision on Wednesday and flash CPI on Thursday. On Friday we receive the final monthly budget balance ahead of the NDO’s forecast on November 26, and on Tuesday there will be a vote in parliament on the Center leader as Prime Minister, which is widely expected to fail.
Norway:
Norges Bank is widely expected to leave its policy rate unchanged at 4.50% at its upcoming rate decision. We expect the Bank to emphasise continued uncertainty around underlying inflation and the risk that elevated external price pressures could slow disinflation, while offering little clues to further guidance. As this is an interim decision, no new projections will be published. Existing home prices have recovered some of the weakness over the summer, although the 3m/3m trend remains broadly flat. We expect modest gains towards year-end and price growth of 3.0% in 2026. Manufacturing production is likely to rebound in September following the previous month’s decline.

articles.title: GDP growth beats expectations, but the picture is mixed
articles.heading: Euro area outlook
articles.fulltext:
The euro area economy beat growth expectations in Q3, expanding by 0.4% Q/Q. Although growth slowed from Q2, the euro area continues to show resilience against the war in the Middle East and higher energy prices. The picture is mixed, however, with Germany and Spain growing faster than expected, while the French economy remains a clear concern.
Key points
Growth in Q3 surprised (for 2nd quarter in row) on the upside
Four consecutive quarters of GDP growth in Germany despite high energy prices
The French economy is a major concern
French GDP fell by 0.1% in Q3 after remaining stable in Q2 and falling in Q1; stagnation and barely avoiding a recession. Germany and Spain both continued to grow, expanding by 0.2% and 0.6%, respectively. Italian GDP was unchanged in Q3. Italian and French GDP were weaker than expected, while Spain and Germany surprised on the upside. Overall, euro area Q3 growth came in at 0.4%, beating our forecast and the consensus estimate of 0.2%. Other member states also posted growth, with Ireland recording the largest quarterly increase at 5.5% (Irish GDP is very volatile). The Netherlands also recorded solid growth of 0.6% in Q3.
Some additional details.
French domestic final demand (excluding inventories) continued to rise, with both household and public consumption increasing. Investment fell again (-0.6%, after -0.5% in Q2). Overall, domestic demand (excluding inventories) contributed 0.1 percentage points to GDP growth, the same as in Q2. The contribution from foreign trade was negative: exports fell by 1.7%, following an increase of 2.8% in Q2, driven by a sharp decline in exports of transport equipment, mainly 
aeronautics
. Imports remained stable. Changes in inventories contributed positively to GDP growth this quarter, following a negative contribution in Q2.
The German Statistical Office (Destatis) reports that final consumption expenditure increased slightly compared with Q2. By contrast, the preliminary figures indicate a decline in investment. The strong export trend seen in H1 2026 slowed noticeably in Q3. Spain continues to outperform its peers, with a large contribution from domestic demand and a small positive contribution from external demand. The election on 29 November is not expected to have any major impact on growth.
The French growth outlook is a major concern
Although growth has held up despite energy-driven inflation and the GDP growth forecast for 2026 is likely to be revised upwards, near-term risks remain tilted to the downside. How the conflict in the Middle East unfolds and when it ends will be critical for the euro area outlook. Business sentiment has remained quite resilient, while consumers remain very cautious, although this caution is not fully reflected in actual spending. The French economy is particularly concerning, with GDP contracting or stagnating in each quarter so far in 2026. Higher energy prices and political turbulence are weighing on growth. Uncertainty surrounding the 2027 budget, the substantial need for fiscal consolidation and the upcoming presidential election are likely to hold back consumer spending and investment, at least during the first half of 2027.

articles.title: No new signals, for now
articles.heading: Norges Bank Preview
articles.fulltext:
Norges Bank is widely expected to leave its policy rate unchanged at 4.50% at its upcoming interim decision on Nov 5. There has been limited new data released since the Sep MPR, and overall developments suggest that inflation risks remain skewed to the upside. We believe the Committee will await more data before reassessing the policy outlook and thus repeat its ‘high for longer’ guidance while simultaneously reiterate a readiness to act if necessary. This will offer the Committee continued flexibility as it neither supports nor dismisses a possible rate hike at the following Dec meeting when new projections will be published. As such, it should not trigger any large market moves. We, however, reiterate that we believe the policy rate peak has been reached.
Policy rate peak likely reached
At its September meeting, Norges Bank hiked the policy rate by 25bps to 4.50%. Uncertainty was high ahead of the decision and minutes confirm that the decision was far from set in stone. Core inflation had surprised markedly on the downside, but the Committee concluded that inflation prospects further out had not changed materially. The rate path was lifted, signalling a 40% chance of another rate hike by March 2027. Rate cuts were also postponed with the path indicating a policy rate of 4.40% end-2027 and 3.90% end-2028. Expectations for the future policy rate path are divided; while we and most domestic forecasters believe the rate peak has been reached, the market discounts another rate hike by next spring. That said, Norges Bank is widely expected to stay on hold at its upcoming interim decision on Nov 5. The rate path did not include any probability of a hike at this meeting and there have been limited new data released since the Sep MPR. Focus will instead be on the Committee’s communication and guidance. 
Norges Banks is facing a tough trade-off between a forceful reaction to inflation having remained above target for several years and avoiding a policy stance that restrict the economy more than needed. Minutes from the September meeting indicated divergent views among board members. Reversing last year’s two rate cuts while signalling a “high for longer” approach appears as a fine-tuned compromise. It also suggests that the bar for raising the policy rate further is high unless the inflation outlook deteriorates materially. This is supported by the Committee’s guidance from September: “…it will likely be necessary to keep the policy rate elevated for a time. The Committee is prepared to raise the policy rate further if warranted by the inflation outlook”. We put emphasis on the Committee’s guidance and regard the 40% likelihood of another hike in the rate path as a hedge should long-term inflation prospects deteriorate significantly. 
We regard the current policy stance and guidance as still being well-balanced. Arguments from both sides within the Committee remain valid; capacity utilization remains below normal, core inflation has eased since before summer, unemployment remains stable, inflation is still too high, and underlying inflation drivers appear little changed. Overall, this makes it hard to see the balance within the Committee shifting at this point. 
Data released since September have been limited and do not deviate substantially from projections. CPI-ATE inflation surprised 0.1ppt on the upside in Sep and given the unexpectedly large downward revision to the bank’s near-term trajectory, we expect core inflation to continue surprising on the upside in coming months. However, the decision to hike rates in September despite inflation having surprised markedly on the downside underscores that it is the long-term inflation prospects that are decisive. This also aligns with the Committee’s reiteration that it will be “particularly attentive to signs that inflation will remain elevated for longer than projected”. The conflict in the Middle East is ongoing and has pushed oil spot and futures prices higher, and European gas prices have also risen ahead of winter. Overall, energy prices are notably higher than assumed in the Sep MPR, and other related prices (e.g., refined oil products, freight rates) remain high. External price pressures thus appear higher, but as this is reflected in a stronger NOK the overall inflation impulse is smaller. Overall, this should support the message from September that risks are skewed to the upside, but we believe the Committee will await more data before concluding that the policy outlook has changed. Ahead of the December decision and MPR, Norges Bank will receive two inflation data releases, the Q4 Inflation Expectations Survey, the national accounts for Q3, and the Regional Network Report – all which will give important input on underlying inflation drivers. As such, we expect Norges Bank to repeat its ‘high for longer’ guidance while simultaneously reiterate a readiness to act if necessary. Given continued substantial uncertainty surrounding developments globally and in energy prices, as well as inflation prospects, this guidance will offer the Committee continued flexibility as it neither supports nor dismisses a possible rate hike at the following December meeting. As such, it should not trigger any large market moves. We, however, reiterate that we believe the policy rate peak has been reached.
Economic developments since September
The upcoming rate decision is an interim decision and will thus not include any new macro projections or rate path, but a press conference will follow the announcement. At interim decisions the Committee evaluates recent economic developments in relation to the assumptions in the MPR, while it usually refrains from drawing any conclusions for the rate path. Below is a summary of developments and data released since Sep26 MPR: 
Global factors:
 Tension in the Middle East have abated though only temporary, as the market awaits the US Mid-term election (Nov 3rd), uncertainty remains high and prospects for any comprehensive settlement remain limited. Energy prices continue to be high and volatile. Both oil spot and futures prices are higher than assumed in the Sep MPR. European natural gas prices have done a similar move, and future prices are also higher, especially for the coming year. In the Business Tendency Survey for 
Q3
, manufacturers reported continued growth in both cost and product prices for both domestic and export markets in Q4. Meanwhile, both long-term government bond yields abroad and market-implied policy rate expectations have corrected somewhat lower since September.
Inflation: 
CPI-ATE inflation was unchanged at 3.0% y/y in 
Sep
, 
slightly below
our own and consensus estimate but 0.1ppt above Norges
Bank’s forecast. Higher-than-expected food prices lifted the figures, and a relatively large decline in furniture prices worked in the opposite direction. The downward revision to the bank’s near-term trajectory in the Sep MPR was surprisingly large, and our forecast is above Norges Bank’s for the coming months. Higher producer prices for food are an upside risk to our forecast. Meanwhile, the stronger NOK will exert downward pressure on imported inflation over the next 12 months, though higher external price impulses will restrain the decline. Though we predict slightly higher core inflation relative to Norges Bank in the next 3-6 months, we forecast lower core inflation later in 2027.  
Wage growth:
 The wage norm was settled at 4.4% this spring, and Norges Bank lowered its annual forecast a notch to 4.4% in Sep following an easing in the quarterly wage statistics. Average monthly earnings data for Q3 will be released on Nov 5, but preliminary monthly data shows that the 3m moving average year-on-year rate eased further to 3.5%from 3.9% in Q2.
Labour market:
 Registered unemployment was stable at 2.0% (SA) in 
Sep
and 
Oct
, after the downward adjustment to the August numbers. Norges Bank’s had projected stable unemployment at 2.1% (SA) for both months, and unemployment is thus running marginally below the Bank’s trajectory for unemployment. Overall, we still argue that the labour market appears broadly stable and the minor discrepancy to Norges Bank’s forecast should not alter its overall outlook on the labour market. At the same, the LFS unemployment is moving sideways at 4.6%, after minor changes to the jobless rate this year. Employment growth according to the LFS survey rose 0.1% q/q in Q3, while preliminary monthly employment data suggest continued flat growth in Q3. Norges Bank estimates employment growth of 0.1% q/q in Q3.
NOK:
 The import-weighted NOK has strengthened throughout the year, albeit surrounded with volatility from the geopolitical backdrop. As tensions in the conflict in the Middle East has heightened so has oil price volatility which has been well reflected in the NOK exchange rate. Nevertheless, the average so far in Q4 is in line with Norges Bank’s forecast after a large depreciation earlier in late September. However, the spot level is 2.8% stronger than the Q1-2027 average, pointing to a larger revision in the Dec MPR.
Fiscal policy:
 The 
2027 budget proposal
implies a slight increase in petroleum revenue spending, although it appears broadly in line with Norges Bank’s expectations. The fiscal impulse is marginally positive, and combined demand impulses from recent budgets will underpin activity. Although fiscal policy will remain a complicating factor for Norges Bank, the budget proposal should not have any direct impact on monetary policy.  
Domestic demand:
 Retail sales ex. autos remained unchanged in 
Q3
, and momentum continues sideways. Softer household demand is mirrored in continued weak consumer confidence and a higher savings ratio. Manufacturing production declined somewhat in 
Aug
, and the average in Jul-Aug points to a negative contribution to the upcoming Q3 national accounts. Meanwhile, the Q3 Business Tendency Survey indicates growing optimism among manufacturers, pointing to stronger production towards year-end. 
Home prices:
 Existing home prices rose 0.3% m/m in 
Sep
, 0.2ppt above Norges Bank’s forecast. Existing home prices have retraced some of the softness seen over the summer and we consider Norges Bank’s annual forecast of 3.0% in 2026 to be reasonable. 
To conclude, inflation has not deviated significantly from projections, but higher external price pressures are adding to upside risks though the NOK has been stronger than assumed. Labour market data appears stable and economic activity has been broadly as envisaged. 
Market implications
Norwegian rates are to a high degree directed by rates abroad. Following the September hike, the market discounted a cumulative 60% chance for a Dec hike and a policy rate peak of 4.75%. The market still discounts almost a full rate hike, though pricing a 50/50 chance between Dec-26 and Mar-27. Given expectations of further rate hikes by the Fed, ECB, Riksbank, etc., we find it reasonable that the market continues to discount near a full hike by Norges Bank. Still, rate hike expectations are not aggressive in a G10 comparison which reflects an already high policy rate level. As stated above, we expect the upcoming decision to be more of a none-event as communication will likely be limited and guidance reiterated. This suggests rather muted market reactions to the announcement, and NOK rates will continue to follow trends abroad. This also implies that any initial reaction in the NOK should be short-lived.

articles.title: Stable unemployment in October
articles.heading: Norwegian unemployment
articles.fulltext:
The seasonal-adjusted registered jobless rate was stable at 2.0% in October and has remained at this level since the downward adjustment of the August numbers. The revision implies that unemployment is run marginally below Norges Bank’s 2.1% estimate. We do not assess this to be alarming as unemployment is trending sideways. Norges Bank expects a marginal rise in the jobless rate from 2027. 
Details
Registered unemployment: 
The unadjusted jobless rate remained stable at 2.0% in October. The seasonal-adjusted unemployment rate was also stable at 2.0% and has remained so since the downward revision to the August numbers. The number of fully unemployed and people on government schemes increased by 400, which nonetheless indicates a stable unemployment rate of 2.6% (SA). In unadjusted terms, fully unemployed persons amounted to 59.1k, part-time unemployed 23.6k and people on employment schemes totalled 13.6k. In total there are now 96.3k persons registered as job seekers in the NAV system. The latter two corresponds to 0.8% and 0.4% of the labour force, respectively.
In October, unemployment either rose or was stable across occupational groups, adjusted for normal seasonal variations. The increase was largest among those with no registered occupational background. The largest decline in unemployment was in construction. Compared to a year ago, two occupational groups stand out at opposite ends of the spectrum. By far the largest increase has been in engineering and ICT, with 800 (18% y/y) more people registered as unemployed or participating in labour market measures. NAV reports that part of the increase is due to the petroleum sector. The largest decline over the past year has been among those with a background in construction, where unemployment has fallen by 700 people (-10% y/y). We do not see this as a sign construction activity is picking up, as many workers in this sector are foreigners and not registered in NAV. Meanwhile, unemployment is highest in travel and transport (3.6%), and lowest among professionals (1.0%).
New registered job vacancies were 34.2k in October, which was 10% higher than a year ago. The 3m/3m trend is negative though NAV reports of a somewhat rising trend recently in the number of vacancies per working day. Vacancies are highest within health care (8.5k) followed by the retail sector (3.6k) and service occupations (3.2k). New registered job vacancies tend to be volatile on a monthly basis, but overall, it points to still healthy labour demand with the long-term trend moving sideways.
Implications Norges Bank:
 Norges Bank expected the registered jobless rate to remain steady at 2.1% for the remainder of the year, rising gradually from Q1 2027 to peak at 2.4% in mid-2028. Due to the revision of the August numbers, unemployment is running 0.1ppt below Norges Bank’s forecast. However, we do not expect this to alter Norges Bank’s assessment of stable and somewhat tight labour market. We expect the policy rate to have peaked in this cycle but argue that it will take some time for rate cuts to start due to sticky and persistent inflation.

articles.title: Stocks fell on AI concerns, ECB and BoJ on hold
articles.heading: Nordic Alert
articles.fulltext:
Global key stories
US stocks fell (S&P 500 -0.3%; Nasdaq -1.4%) after lower-than-expected results from 
Alphabet
, among others, which added to concerns about valuations in the AI sector. This prompted investors to look for safer assets such as Treasuries as well as the Swiss franc and Japanese yen. Crude oil prices rose after media reports continued to suggest that the US may resume military strikes against Iran. Yesterday, the 
Wall Street Journal
 published an article that the president had been notified of possible future military options in Iran. The euro strengthened against the dollar while the price of gold fell below $4,000 per ounce and was on track for its lowest closing level for gold since mid-July. In Asia, the Tokyo Stock Exchange opens lower and the Chinese indices rise this morning. 
The ECB kept rates on hold and Lagarde will leave in February.
 Yesterday, the ECB chose to keep the interest rate unchanged, without any commitments on future measures. Nothing in the decision or the press release rules out another interest rate hike in December. In connection with the meeting, Christine Lagarde also announced that she will resign in February next year. (See our comment 
here
).
The BoJ signalled inflation risks despite tighter monetary policy.
 The Bank of Japan's (BoJ) widely expected decision to leave interest rates on Friday morning was accompanied by a relatively hawkish economic forecast that continued to point to the risk that inflation could exceed the target. The BoJ assessed that underlying inflation is "broadly consistent" with the 2 per cent target for the first time since the inflation target was introduced in 2013. It also maintained its view that inflation risks are on the upside, despite the interest rate hike in September and the hawkish reversal in monetary policy.
GDP, inflation and the ECB's analyst survey. Today,
 flash estimates of both October's inflation and third-quarter GDP are published for several of the major countries in the euro area. In Norway, unemployment data for October and Norges Bank's foreign exchange trading for November are released. In Colombia, the central bank is expected to keep the policy rate unchanged. The ECB also publishes its quarterly Survey of Professional Forecasters with updated projections for inflation, growth and unemployment. Japan's core inflation for October, released just after midnight, came in at 2.6% and slightly lower than expected.
The final vote count in the Israeli election
, which 
was announced 
early Friday local time, confirmed that neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition nor the main opposition alliance received enough seats to form a government. The result is likely to mean several weeks of power struggles and political uncertainty. A stalemate in the political negotiations means that Netanyahu will continue as acting prime minister until a new government is formed. 
Worth reading from SEB
: 
US GDP
 and 
SEB FI & FX Strategy
. Today we also published our 
SEB Latin America Outlook
, where we update the forecasts for Brazil and Mexico. 
Nordic key stories
The krona strengthened against the euro yesterday and the OMX30 rose 0.4%.
New investor survey from SEB.
 The vast majority of people in our Investor Survey believe that the interest rate will be raised next week, but a small minority believe that the interest rate will remain unchanged. Almost everyone believes that the interest rate will remain (or be raised) to 2% in December, and by March, as many as 95% believe that the Riksbank will have raised interest rates by at least 50 basis points compared to today. Half of the investors believe that the Riksbank says that the upside risks for the interest rate path have increased since September, while the rest believe that the Executive Board signals that the risks are unchanged. here
.

articles.title: Börsen föll på fortsatt AI-oro, ECB och BoJ sitter still
articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
Börsen i USA föll (S&P 500 -0,3%; Nasdaq -1,4%) efter lägre än väntade resultat från bland annat 
Alphabet
, som spädde på oron för värderingar inom AI-sektorn. Detta fick investerare att söka sig mot säkrare tillgångar såsom amerikanska statsobligationer samt schweizerfrancen och japanska yenen. Råoljepriset steg efter medieuppgifter som fortsatt tyder på att USA kan komma att återuppta militära attacker mot Iran. Igår publicerade 
Wall Street Journal
 en artikel om att presidenten underrättats om möjliga framtida militära alternativ i Iran. Euron stärktes mot dollarn medan guldpriset sjönk under 4 000 dollar per uns och var på väg mot sin lägsta stängningsnivå för guld sedan mitten av juli. I Asien öppnar Tokyobörsen ned och de kinesiska indexen uppåt nu på morgonen. 
ECB sitter still och Lagarde lämnar i februari.
 Igår valde ECB efter enhälligt beslut att hålla räntan oförändrad, utan några åtaganden om framtida åtgärder. Inget i beslutet eller pressmeddelandet utesluter ytterligare en räntehöjning i december. I samband med mötet meddelade också Christine Lagarde att hon avgår i februari nästa år. (Läs mer i vår kommentar 
här
). 
BoJ signalerade inflationsrisker trots stramare penningpolitik.
 Den japanska centralbankens (BoJ) allmänt förväntade beslut nu på fredagsmorgonen att lämna räntan åtföljdes av en relativt hökaktig konjunkturprognos som fortsatt pekade på risken att inflationen kan överskrida målet. BoJ bedömde att den underliggande inflationen för första gången sedan inflationsmålet infördes 2013 är ”i stort sett förenlig” med målet på 2 procent. Man vidhöll också sin uppfattning att inflationsriskerna är uppåtriktade, trots räntehöjningen i september och den hökaktiga omsvängningen i penningpolitiken.
BNP, inflation och ECB:s analytikerundersökning.
 Idag publiceras flashestimat på både oktobers inflation och tredje kvartalets BNP för flera av de större länderna i euroområdet. I Norge släpps arbetslöshetsdata för oktober samt Norges Banks valutahandel för november. I Colombia väntas centralbanken hålla styrräntan oförändrad. ECB publicerar också sin kvartalsvisa Survey of Professional Forecasters med uppdaterade projektioner för inflation, tillväxt och arbetslöshet. Japans kärninflation för oktober, som släpptes strax efter midnatt, blev 2,6% och något lägre än väntat.
Den slutliga rösträkningen i det israeliska valet
, som 
offentliggjordes 
tidigt på fredagen lokal tid, bekräftade att varken premiärminister Benjamin Netanyahus koalition eller den största oppositionsalliansen fick tillräckligt många mandat för att bilda en regering. Resultatet innebär sannolikt flera veckors maktkamp och politisk osäkerhet. Ett dödläge i de politiska förhandlingarna innebär att Netanyahu fortsätter som tillförordnad premiärminister tills en ny regering bildats.

: 
Amerikansk BNP
 och

SEB Latin America Outlook
, där vi uppdaterar prognoserna för Brasilien och Mexiko.

articles.title: Transition to a demand-driven Eurosystem
articles.heading: SEB FI & FX Strategy
articles.fulltext:
At a glance:
In market focus.
 Earnings season; euro area October inflation (from 30 October); US mid-terms (3 November); geopolitics; Upcoming French government bond auctions (next: 5 November).
Global macro and risk appetite.
 Over the past month, the benign backdrop for equities has come under pressure from three simultaneous shocks: rapidly rising oil prices, spillovers into broader euro area bond markets from France’s political and fiscal turbulence, and doubts about the sustainability of the AI capex boom. Beneath the noise, however, the fundamental story remains intact. Macro data are holding up on both sides of the Atlantic and Q3 earnings are also encouraging, with positive surprises continuing to dominate in the US and globally. This suggests the recent turbulence may yet prove to be noise rather than a turning point, but only if these concerns subside. US midterm elections have historically been followed by strong equity returns, and we see a positive post-election performance as a likely outcome this year, too.
US macro: Booming economy, elevated inflation. 
The US economy grew well above most estimates for trend in Q3, supported by very firm consumer spending and AI-related investments. Core PCE inflation is increasing again after the downward revision in August and remains well above the 2%-target. This should not be a surprise to the Fed but remains a dilemma. We continue to expect a slowdown in consumer spending as the support from unusually large tax refunds fades, while positive wealth effects continue to support spending. The strong reliance on AI investments and wealthy households make US growth sensitive to changes in the views on the AI expansion and equity market performance, but for now the data supports that policy is not restrictive.
USD short rates: Dovish reactions to the FOMC meeting. 
As expected, the Fed left policy unchanged on 28 October, with two members dissenting in favour of a 25bp hike. The main surprise was Chair Warsh’s softer press-conference language, where he said the Fed had made progress in tightening financial conditions since September. We see this as supporting a December hike but leaving the subsequent path uncertain. The statement contained no changes to balance-sheet policy. Warsh has previously called for renewed balance-sheet reduction, but any changes will have to wait until next year.
USD bonds: Range-bound.
 Concerns over AI-related stocks and rising energy prices have driven a rotation into bonds, lowering long-end yields and flattening the curve. With forwards pricing in around 70bp of rate hikes, we see scope for policy rate expectations to soften over time, supporting bonds. We expect the 10Y Treasury yield to trade mostly near 5% in the coming weeks.
France: Key milestones in the budget process.
 The government submitted its draft budget to the National Assembly in early October. The Assembly first examines revenue, with scrutiny extended into early November, before turning to expenditure. The vote on the full draft was originally scheduled for 17 November, marking the end of the Assembly’s standard 40-day scrutiny period. The voting timetable remains provisional, however. The Senate will consider the budget in late November and December. The 70-day deadline for parliamentary approval expires on 17 December. Given the fragmented parliament, it remains uncertain whether the budget will secure approval.
EUR short rates: Wait and see. 
Yesterday’s ECB meeting echoed recent Governing Council comments that tighter financial conditions may reduce the need for rate hikes, while reaffirming that the ECB has tools to counter unwarranted market dynamics. Forwards price in nearly 70bp of rate hikes by autumn 2027. We see scope for this to fall below 60bp in the coming months with the next hike expected in December.
ECB: Transition to a demand-driven Eurosystem.
 The ECB is currently reviewing its operational framework as the Eurosystem transitions from ample excess liquidity to a demand-driven system, where banks are expected to make active use of refinancing operations. We expect new structural refinancing operations to be introduced in late 2027, followed by a structural securities portfolio in 2028.
EUR bonds: Softer policy outlook caps yields. 
The French-German 10Y spread has narrowed from last week’s peak of 175bp to around 155bp, but the risk of renewed turbulence is likely to persist for months. Softer ECB expectations since late September have helped push the German 10Y yield lower and we expect it to trade mostly in the 3.30-3.50% range in the coming weeks.
EUR/USD: 
Middle East back in focus after the midterms.
Markets are pricing a Democratic sweep in the 3 November midterms. If the result is in line with expectations, we expect limited lasting impact on EUR/USD, and focus should shift back to the Middle East. On the Euro side, France remains the main risk, with budget milestones in November and December – with the France presidential election in 2027 as the more decisive event and expect a muddle-through until then.

ECB: Transition to a demand-driven Eurosystem
In 
SEB FI & FX Strategy
 on 16 October, we discussed how we expect the ECB to respond to euro area fragmentation should the need arise. Since then, the ECB has further softened its rhetoric, signalling that tighter financial conditions will reduce the need for rate hikes. Yesterday’s meeting reiterated this message and stressed that the ECB has tools to counter fragmentation if needed.
Below, we discuss the ongoing operational framework review, which is expected to clarify plans for the structural refinancing operations and structural securities portfolio the ECB has said it will introduce. These structural programmes are part of a separate process and should not be confused with the ECB’s tools for managing fragmentation.
Operational framework review ongoing. The ECB is reviewing its March 2024 operational framework as the Eurosystem moves from abundant liquidity towards a demand-driven regime. Excess liquidity is still high, at around EUR 2.1tn, and banks can source overnight liquidity at rates close to the deposit facility rate (DFR), leaving little incentive to borrow at the main refinancing operation (MRO) rate, currently DFR+15bp.
EUR short rates
We expect the ECB to publish its operational-framework review in H1 2027, introduce structural refinancing operations no earlier than late 2027 and begin building a structural securities portfolio only in 2028.
What could the operational-framework review cover?
 H1 2027 may be too early for the ECB to disclose the full details of its planned structural operations. Nevertheless, the review could outline:
Structural refinancing operations: 
Maturity, frequency, collateral framework and tender procedure for structural refinancing operations, alongside pricing (likely to be linked to the realised MRO rate over the life of each operation plus a spread).
Structural securities portfolio:
 Eligible securities, maturity guidelines and technical details such as risk sharing.
The recent 
Bank of Finland report
 suggests that the size of the structural securities portfolio could be calibrated jointly with structural refinancing operations, as both will contribute to meeting the banking system’s durable liquidity demand. We do not expect the review to disclose a firm target size for the securities portfolio.
What will determine the timing and scale?
 The ECB intends to introduce the new operations once it sees durable demand for liquidity through regular refinancing operations. It has stated that structural longer-term refinancing operations and a structural securities portfolio will be introduced once the Eurosystem balance sheet begins to grow durably again. The timing will depend on several interrelated factors.
The pace of APP and PEPP redemptions.
 Continued portfolio run-off drains reserves from the banking system.
Banks’ demand for reserves.
 Demand will be shaped by payment flows, precautionary liquidity preferences, regulation, collateral practices and the uneven distribution of reserves across jurisdictions and institutions.
Take-up in existing refinancing operations.
 Rising, broad-based use of regular MROs and longer-term refinancing operations (LTROs) would signal that the system is becoming operationally demand-driven.
Money-market functioning.
 A gradual firming of repo rates and €STR relative to the DFR would be consistent with money market normalisation. The ECB is unlikely to react mechanically to fluctuations in repo and other money market rates, provided rate volatility does not obscure the policy signal or impair transmission.
On volumes, the ECB has indicated that future structural longer-term refinancing operations and a structural securities portfolio will make a substantial contribution to meeting the banking sector’s structural liquidity needs arising from autonomous factors – principally banknotes in circulation and government deposits – and minimum reserve requirements.
Regular refinancing operations (MRO & LTRO)
How could the new operations be designed? 
Structural refinancing operations will precede securities purchases. We expect the following key features:
Structural refinancing operations.
 Their maturities should help meet banks’ predictable liquidity needs without displacing regular money-market activity, particularly repos. We expect these operations to be longer-dated than the existing three-month LTROs, with maturities of one year or longer. Longer residual maturities would provide available stable funding under the net stable funding ratio (NSFR), although the net benefit would depend on the operation’s maturity, repayment options and the treatment of pledged collateral. One possible design would involve regular, potentially quarterly, tranches, with volumes increased gradually as the Eurosystem gains a clearer picture of durable reserve demand, as also discussed in the recent Bank of Finland analysis.
Structural securities portfolio. 
The ECB has indicated that purchases should begin only once it has greater confidence in the scale of durable liquidity demand and how much of that demand refinancing operations will meet. The portfolio would provide a stable component of reserve supply, maintained over time through reinvestments.
Structural operations should not be confused with QE.
 The structural securities portfolio is intended as a balance-sheet-management instrument, rather than a renewed QE programme or a tool for controlling intra-euro-area spreads.
While the ECB plans to let its APP and PEPP holdings run off naturally, we think it could temporarily resume APP and/or PEPP reinvestments in the event of more severe euro area fragmentation. However, we expect the first line of defence to be softer rhetoric and fewer rate hikes than would otherwise be warranted. Our expectations for the ECB’s response and sequencing in the event of euro-area fragmentation were discussed in 
Euro area fragmentation risk: How will the ECB respond?
, published on 16 October.
Implications for money-market rates.
 As the transition towards a demand-driven framework progresses, we expect €STR to rise to 1-3bp above the DFR by end-2028. Over the same period, we expect the overnight RFR Euro one-day repo rate to rise from around 2.5bp above the DFR currently to 8-12bp above it by end-2028.
As the ECB has stated, a moderate rise in market rates relative to the DFR is a feature of a functioning demand-driven framework. The MRO should provide a backstop for eligible banks, although collateral, balance-sheet and access constraints can still allow individual market rates to trade above the MRO rate. We expect the ECB to look through temporary quarter-end repo spikes, provided money-market functioning and policy transmission remain orderly.
Implications for swap spreads. 
For German government bonds vs 6M Euribor swaps, the outlook depends on the relative moves in German bond yields vs €STR swaps and in the €STR/6M Euribor basis. We expect repo rates to rise relative to €STR in 2027, supporting higher German government bond yields vs €STR swaps. At the same time, the €STR/6M Euribor basis should remain wide and could widen further until liquidity conditions stabilise and the France-related turbulence eases.
Therefore, we initially expect German government bonds to remain rich and potentially richen further relative to 6M Euribor swaps. At a later stage of a transition to the demand-driven Eurosystem, higher repo rates and a stabilising basis should support a cheapening of German government bonds relative to 6M Euribor swaps. We expect the German 10Y government bond yield to trade flat vs 6M Euribor swaps within two years.
German government yields – 6M Euribor swaps (maturity matched spread, bp)
Source: Bloomberg, SEB.
EURUSD: Middle East back in focus after the midterms
Markets are pricing a Democratic sweep
Polls and betting markets point to a Democratic House and a narrow Democratic Senate, with a sweep priced at around 65%. A divided Congress would make further tax cuts less likely, but in our view not enough to change the USD outlook. Midterms have historically been followed by strong equity returns, which would modestly support EUR. A contested result could initially support USD on risk-off, but a prolonged dispute would more likely weigh on USD via institutional uncertainty.
After midterms, focus is likely to shift back to escalation versus de-escalation in the Middle East
Reports of US briefings to Gulf allies on post-midterm military action could reflect an actual plan, or positioning ahead of negotiations. Escalation would likely support USD via safe-haven demand and higher oil prices. De-escalation would lower oil and remove an important USD support. With both the Fed and ECB expected to hike in December, and both curves likely to soften over time, we think oil and risk sentiment matter more than rate differentials near term.
France remains a risk for EUR
The French–German 10y spread has narrowed from 175bp to around 155bp, but the budget process is still ahead of us, making it the main euro-specific risk near term. The Assembly vote is provisionally scheduled for 17 November and the deadline for parliamentary approval is 17 December. With a fragmented parliament, approval is uncertain. A failed budget would likely widen spreads again and weigh on EUR, while approval could ease some pressure. The 2027 presidential election is probably the more decisive event.
Our CTA proxy shows positioning close to maximum short EURUSD. With positioning this stretched, progress on the French budget or signs of de-escalation in the Middle East could give relief for EUR, while larger EUR downside would likely require a stronger catalyst.

articles.title: Almost all expect a hike in November
articles.heading: SEB Investor Survey
articles.fulltext:
*** See attachment for full report ***
Riksbank expected to hike to 2.00% in November
A wide majority (90%) of respondents expect the Riksbank to raise the policy rate to 2.00% in November. 
A minority of 10% predict the policy rate to be unchanged at 1.75%.
Most responds predict the policy rate to remain at (or be raised to) 2.00% in December. Slightly more than 20% predict that the policy rate will be raised to 2.25%, while 5% predict the rate to remain at 1.75%. 
The survey was conducted between October 27-29 among large Swedish fixed income investors.
A wide majority predict at least 2 rate hikes by March
Almost all (95%), expect at least two rate hikes by March next year. 
Most (almost 80%) expect two hikes to 2.25%. 
Around 15% expects three hikes to 2.50%. 
A thin minority (5%) predicts unchanged rates at 1.75%.
Further out, expectations continue to diverge substantially. In December 2027, expectations span 1.25-3.00%. 
The median expectation in December 2027 has increased to 2.5%, which is 25bps higher than in the September survey.

articles.title: Disinflation amid a wide set of risks
articles.heading: Latin America Outlook
articles.fulltext:
Brazil: 
Lula reelection upset comes with fiscal and market risks  
A post-election slowdown is coming, and growth should remain around 2% throughout our forecast horizon.
Inflation has trended upward but will converge to target.
The election outcome has shut the door to further monetary easing this year and, provided fiscal risks are resolved, this should allow the policy rate to decline to 12.5% by end of 2027.
Markets will require significant steps toward fiscal reform in the near term, but we expect the government will underdeliver, leaving the real flat going forward.
Mexico: Fundamentals drive compressed policy rate differentials
Overall, the economic story for Mexico in 2026 is one of gradual recovery, with some signs of greater momentum looking ahead. A downside risk to growth is that the government delivers more fiscal consolidation than we foresee.
Disinflation to progress gradually and we expect 3.8% and 3.5% inflation for 2026 and 2027.
Banxico will remain on hold throughout our forecast horizon, consistent with gradual disinflation which should allow more compressed policy rate differentials.
We therefore see room for a somewhat stronger peso in 2027, but markets could remain skeptical over geopolitical and trade risks.

articles.title: Booming growth, supported by strong AI and very resilient consumer demand
articles.heading: US Economy
articles.fulltext:
US GDP growth accelerated to an annualized 3.4% q/q in q3 (consensus 3.2%, previous 2.2%). Underlying demand was very firm, with consumer spending expanding by 3.8% q/q annualised and business investments by 13%. US core PCE inflation increased in September in line with expectations. The strong growth should not come as a surprise for the Fed, which upgraded its views on the economy in yesterday’s policy statement. Still, the data supports at least one more rate hike most likely at the December meeting, with the prospects for further hikes thereafter more uncertain. 
Key points
Q3 GDP accelerated from 2.2 to 3.4% q/q, annualized, above the consensus (3.2%)
Very firm underlying growth. Final private domestic demand increased by 4.9%
Personal consumption increased by 3.8% (consensus 3.4%)
AI investments continue to drive equipment spending
Core PCE inflation increased by 0.3% m/m, 3.1% y/y in September, in line with consensus
Strong GDP growth despite large drag from foreign trade
US growth beat expectations in Q3 with a stronger-than-expected 3.4% q/q annualized growth (consensus 3.2%). Underlying consumer and business demand was very strong, with the latter two sectors expanding at a combined pace of 4.9% in Q3, up from 4.6% in Q2. Personal consumption spending was the main contributor (2.5%-points), followed by fixed non-residential investments (1.8%-points), inventories (1.6%-points) and (federal) government spending (0.9%-points). These were offset by a decline in exports and a strong increase in imports (which deducts from GDP), leading to a large net negative contribution from foreign trade (-3.3%-points).
The AI build-out continues to drive investments, with very solid contributions to GDP from IP equipment (0.9%-points) and IP products (0.5%-points) but there are signs that other equipment investments are contributing more to growth (industrial equipment contributed 0.3%-points, similar to in Q2).  
Strength in consumption may be partly temporary
Some of the strength of spending in Q3 may be temporary. US personal spending has been supported by unusually large tax refunds stemming from last year's tax cuts which were not fully paid out last year. This effect should be fading, while high gasoline prices will continue to weigh on purchasing power. Strong wealth effects have also supported spending among wealthier households, which has been reflected in a decline in the savings rate below the historical averages. This makes consumption sensitive to any shifts in equity markets, including views on companies and sectors more related to the rapid advancement in AI. The strong advance in personal consumption in Q3 reflected very strong increases in August, which was followed by flat spending in September.
The personal savings rate (3.8%) has been trending gradually lower over the past 2 ½ - 3 years and is well below the pre-pandemic (2014-2019) average of 6.2%. Recurring upward revisions of incomes have lifted the savings rate compared to preliminary estimates this year, but the current level is still the lowest since 2022, when household spending was supported by earlier pandemic support payments.  
No signs of slowdown in AI investments
AI-related investments have been volatile on a quarterly basis but do not show any signs of slowing yet. However, the build-out of data centers also depends on importing IT hardware from Asia, which is currently boosting imports but probably also private inventories. Construction of data centers is also contributing to rising investments in structures (0.15% q/q in Q3). Residential construction declined again (-0.1% q/q), not unexpectedly given the increase in rates.
The Fed’s key inflation measure remains too high, as expected 
Core PCE inflation increased by 0.3% m/m, 3.1% y/y in September, in line with the consensus. The y/y rate increased slightly after a larger than expected downward effect from the pre-announced revisions in late September and it remains well above the 2%-inflation target. The Fed is usually good at estimating the core PCE, based on input from the CPI and PPI. That core PCE continues to increase at a pace above what is consistent with the 2% target remains a dilemma, however.
The Fed has upgraded its views on growth
The strong GDP data should not come as a surprise to the Fed, which upgraded its language on economic activity in its October policy statement. We also note that Warsh in his press conference did not suggest that the economy was overheating and thus signalling a need for the Fed to slow the economy to get inflation under control. Still, strong growth supports the message that financial conditions are not tight and that the Fed has more work to do to reach a neutral level. 
We continue to expect the Fed to deliver another rate increase at the December meeting. The pace thereafter is uncertain and will depend on the conflict in the Middle East and risks for price pressures in energy and IT equipment spreading to other sectors. We will present updated forecasts for the US economy and the Fed after the midterm elections next week.

articles.title: Unchanged rates – for now
articles.heading: ECB Review
articles.fulltext:
The ECB left its key policy rates unchanged at its 29 October meeting. The decision was unanimous, with no commitment to future action, as the ECB reiterated its data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach. The ECB stressed heightened upside inflation risks and looked ahead to a more in-depth analysis in December. Nothing in the decision or communication rules out another rate hike in December.
Key points
Unchanged policy rates with the deposit rate remaining at 2.50%
Heightened of indirect and second-round effects highlighted
Confirmation that financial conditions play a key role in the coming months
According to the press release, rising energy prices pose upside risks to inflation and downside risks to growth. Underlying inflation remains broadly stable, with no significant wage response so far. However, a larger and more prolonged energy shock increases the risk of indirect and second-round effects. Tighter financing conditions are also likely to weigh on both growth and inflation.
Key conclusions from the Q&A at the press conference
Although a rate hike was debated, the Governing Council unanimously agreed that the ECB was sufficiently well positioned to keep interest rates unchanged for now
Upcoming data (inflation, GDP, PMI etc.) and December staff projections will be extremely relevant for underlying inflation.
The ECB has instruments available to handle unwarranted market movements.
Another hike is still on the table.
Not surprisingly a lot of questions during the press conference centered on President Lagarde’s decision to leave on 7 February 2027. Indeed, as we wrote in our preview this starts as a political process within the EU to form a new puzzle of key ECB positions, read more 
here
.

articles.title: Ahead of October CPI
articles.heading: Swedish inflation
articles.fulltext:
Core inflation expected to edge lower in October
CPIF ex energy
 is predicted to slow to edge lower to 0.4% y/y in October (September 0.5% y/y, Riksbank forecast: 0.6% y/y). 
CPIF 
is expected to slow to 1.4% y/y (September 1.5% y/y Riksbank: 1.5% y/y). Both electricity and fuel prices rose sharply in September but were largely stable in October.
CPIF ex energy
 corrected for lower VAT and the increased subsidy for public transport is also expected to move marginally lower to 1.4% y/y (September 1.5% y/y, Riksbank forecast 1.7% y/y).
Lower core inflation in October, but upward trend
CPIF excluding energy is expected to edge lower in October, leaving core inflation 0.2 percentage points below the Riksbanks’s forecast following September’s downside surprise. Slightly lower price hikes on international travels are expected to exert downward pressure, while goods inflation is expected to accelerate somewhat. 
There are still no clear signs of indirect effects from high energy prices, with producer prices on consumer goods and pricing plans in the NIER survey remaining largely stable. Rising electronics prices, driven by strong AI-related demand, pose an upside risk to inflation in October. Looking ahead, indirect effects from high energy prices and a weaker SEK are expected to push inflation higher over the next 6–12 months. CPIF excluding energy, adjusted for the VAT cut and public transport subsidies, is expected to temporarily rise above the 2% target during spring and summer.
Largely stable energy prices in October
Energy prices are predicted to rise by 0.5-1% in October, driven by higher fuel prices, while electricity prices are set to decline slightly. Electricity prices have fallen significantly over the past two weeks, while fuel prices have also edged lower. As a result, our forecast for headline inflation in October has been lowered by 0.3pp compared with our forecast following the September CPI release. However, the relief from lower energy prices is likely to be temporary, as electricity futures prices for autumn and winter have increased from already elevated levels. The reversal of temporary fuel tax cuts will push fuel prices up by 3-4% in October and by almost another 15% in December. Headline CPIF inflation is therefore expected to rise significantly above target in December.
Policy implications
The Riksbank was more hawkish than expected in September, and the minutes confirmed that a rate hike in November is highly likely. None of the Executive Board members discussed the possibility of hiking in both November and December, but markets continue to price a relatively high probability of two hikes this year. We maintain our forecast for rate hikes in November, February and May. The recent partial unwinding of aggressive market pricing for near-term rate hikes by the ECB and the Fed lends some support to our forecast. However, uncertainty has increased following the notable hawkish shift in September. Actual inflation outcomes, developments in the Middle East and policy decisions by other central banks will determine the timing and extent of further rate hikes.

articles.title: Why, how much and their NOK impact
articles.heading: Norges Bank FX transactions
articles.fulltext:
We expect Norges Bank to increase their monthly net FX purchases to NOK 626 million per day in November, up from NOK 176 million in October. The increase of NOK 450 million is due to the expectation that Norges Bank will use the updated estimate for the 2026 non-oil budget deficit, as published in the 2027 budget proposal. The updated estimate of NOK 454.8 bn is NOK 16.4 bn lower than the previous official figure and signals less need for NOK to cover the deficit. Forecasting Norges Bank FX transactions involves many moving parts, however. This note therefore explains why Norges Bank does such transactions and presents an updated SEB framework for estimating them, and reviews what the contributing factors have been for the changes from month-to-month this year.
Norges Bank transacts daily in the FX markets for two purposes.
 The first, and most important one, is to make the appropriate exchanges related to spending of petroleum revenue. This part is done on behalf of the Ministry of Finance as a ‘banking service’, and not for any central banking purposes. These transactions are the ones that may vary considerably from month to month. The second purpose for the daily transactions is to convert FX income from the central bank’s FX reserves to NOK, in order to fund the transfer of Norges Bank dividends and interest payments to the government. This part is static for 12 months at a time and is expected to change little from year to year. This note focuses on the first type of FX transactions, related to the petroleum revenue.
The petroleum revenue-related transactions 
arise from the setup with the Norwegian ‘petroleum fund mechanism’. In short, this is an accounting and spending framework that states that all of the government’s petroleum-related revenue belongs to the Global Pension Fund Global (GPFG, or the ‘oil fund’) first, and that the government may only use some of this (as set by the 3% fiscal policy rule) to cover the non-oil budget deficits. The reason this creates a need for exchanging currencies is that the non-oil budget deficit is in NOK, while the petroleum revenues are both in NOK and foreign exchange. The government receives NOK revenues from oil taxes and dividend/buybacks from Equinor and foreign currency revenues from the government's own petroleum activities via the State's Direct Financial Interest (SDFI). If the NOK revenues aren’t sufficient to cover the deficit, FX revenue needs to be converted to NOK. Conversely, if NOK revenues are larger than the deficit, this needs to be exchanged to FX in order to be transferred to the GPFG.
[1]
 Hence, the two most important drivers of FX transactions are (a) the size of petroleum-related revenue in NOK, and (b) the government’s non-oil budget deficit.
Norges Bank announces the needs for any FX transactions on a monthly basis.
 At the end of each month, the central bank takes stock of any relevant input and decides on the daily amount they are going to sell or buy in the market every business day in the coming month. Their calculations are based on the needs for the calendar year, taking already exchanged amounts into account. The amount they decide on is then what would be needed to be exchanged not only in the coming month, but every trading day for the remainder of the year, given no new information emerges. Daily transaction volumes are then fixed for the month, and new information will only affect purchases from the following month.
Forecasting Norges Bank FX transactions
 is a rather technical exercise, but also requires some judgement. The technical bit consists of gathering relevant numbers from different data sources and government documents. These include changes in forward oil and gas prices, revisions to estimates for petroleum tax payments and the non-oil budget deficit, dividends and buy-backs from Equinor, and petroleum investments (e.g. costs related to SDFI), amongst other things.
The judgement part largely consists of making a call on when cut-off dates for petroleum tax estimates are made, and how Norges Bank relate to new information, potentially having to choose between input from different government agencies (such as this month, see more below).
A new SEB framework aims to forecast what Norges Bank will be publishing as their daily FX transactions in the coming month, and making the changes between months more transparent. 
The framework has recently been established, but the chart below shows what the model would have estimated throughout the year, based on publicly available information at the time. Chart 1 shows that the model does a good job directionally and also has a reasonably good fit, with its largest misses in months with significant changes in the amounts, such as April.
Chart 1: Announced daily petroleum revenue-related FX transactions and model estimates (excluding the transactions for transfers of dividends and interest rates)
For instance, an increase in expected petroleum taxes was unsurprisingly behind the reduced NOK purchases in April, as petroleum prices spiked in March. The same dynamic repeated itself in the autumn, and for November, it is the mentioned reduction in the estimated non-oil budget deficit that is the driver (see below).
Chart 2 below shows what the contributing factors have been behind the changes in the monthly amounts in 2026. Unsurprisingly, it is clear that changes in petroleum tax and the non-oil budget deficit are the main drivers behind the changes. The latter is updated when new budget estimates arrive from the budgetary process. Meanwhile, the petroleum tax is a more continuous contributor, as the fluctuation in forward prices impacts estimates of tax payments for the second half of the year. This is due to taxes being paid with a 6-month lag (i.e., taxes for 2026 are paid during H2-2026 and H1-2027).
Chart 2: Decomposition of contributions to monthly changes in FX transactions
For November
, we expect Norges Bank to increase its daily FX purchases to NOK 750mn from 300mn, implying net FX purchases of NOK 626mn. The 2027 budget proposal estimated petroleum taxes of NOK 389bn in 2026, which we find surprisingly low considering that The Norwegian Tax Administration updated its estimate in a press release August 31st which points to NOK 430bn. It appears as if the government has not included this update in the budget, and we therefore expect Norges Bank to overlook this and keep the petroleum tax estimate unchanged. Meanwhile, the non-oil budget deficit was reduced by NOK 16.4bn. This implies that more NOK revenues must be converted into foreign currency for transfer to the GPFG. With only six weeks of FX transactions remaining in 2026, the impact on FX purchases from such a revision should be substantial.
For 2027
, the current budget proposal suggests a large need for Norges Bank to buy NOK on a daily basis to fund the deficit. This is due to the non-oil budget deficit increasing by NOK 107bn to 562bn, while petroleum tax income is expected to fall to NOK 359bn. However, just as for 2026, the tax estimate appears significantly outdated. Ahead of the January announcement of FX transactions, Norges Bank will receive updated estimates for both the deficit and petroleum taxes in the finally approved budget in early December. Further adjustments are likely in February as The Norwegian Tax Administration publishes its final estimate on petroleum taxes for 2026 in late January (to be paid in H1 2027).
NOK impact is decided by the deficit and dependent on timing.
Norges Bank's FX transactions have drawn a lot of attention due to its potential impact on the NOK. The impact mainly stems from timing mismatches between flows, and in particular related to petroleum taxes. Oil companies are active in the market daily to buy NOK ahead of tax installments and can quickly adopt to large swings in oil and gas prices. Though Norges Bank’s flow is offsetting this effect, they come with a lag as the bank is largely dependent on public information and revises their transactions only once a month. For example, not until September did Norges Bank switch from buying to selling NOK, and net flows from oil companies and Norges Bank have thus been supportive for most of this year. This is now turning as Norges Bank is catching up with large NOK-selling towards year-end.
Chart 3: Norges Bank's daily FX purchases, NOK
Since all petroleum revenues are generated in FX, and all excess revenues are transferred to the GPFG, these mismatching flows are only having a temporary impact on the NOK. Ultimately, what matters for the krone is the size of the non-oil budget deficit. This determines the amount of NOK that actually ‘stays in the economy’, and the change in the deficit from one year to another represents the net inflow of NOK from the petroleum mechanism. For 2026, this implied a NOK 21bn NOK-outflow, while the 2027 budget proposal implies a NOK 107bn NOK-inflow.
Chart 4: Net NOK inflows are decided by the non-oil budget deficit
In practice, however, the impact is much smaller as a widening non-oil budget deficit is mirrored in a wider mainland trade deficit. Consequently, much of the petroleum revenue spent domestically ultimately leaks out through higher imports.
Chart 5: Norwegian mainland trade deficit
[1]
 Technically, Norges Bank handles FX transactions and transfers to and from the GPFG through a separate ‘petrobuffer’ portfolio (PBP).

articles.title: Firm growth in Q3 GDP according to volatile preliminary estimate
articles.heading: Swedish growth
articles.fulltext:
Despite a decline in October for the monthly indicator (-0.7%, 2.1% y/y), flash GDP increased largely in line with our and the consensus estimate in Q3. Growth in August and September were revised slightly higher. The Q3 reading was marginally higher than the Riksbank’s forecast. Flash GDP is not a very reliable predictor for final GDP (presented on November 27), but indicators of household consumption and private sector production support that growth remained firm in Q3. Many growth metrics suggest that risks to the 
flash
 estimate are skewed to the upside. 
Growth in 2026 is set to exceed our forecast (2.7%) but risks for growth in 2027 are shifting clearly to the downside. A sharp decline in consumer confidence shows that households are coming under pressure from rising energy prices. Moreover, the energy prices will become substantially higher over the next 3-4 months, with a reversal of fuel tax cuts adding on an increase in global energy market prices. Early rate hikes from the Riksbank will add further dampening pressure on households in the beginning of next year. 
Retail sales declined slightly in September (-0.4%, 5.5% y/y, previous 0.9%, 7.2% y/y, SEB forecast 0.5%, 6.2% y/y), but August was revised higher and the decline comes on the back of exceptionally strong growth over the last 6 months. Retailers continued to be optimistic in October, but a sharp decline for consumer confidence increases the risk for a setback over the coming quarter.
